title: A Tale of Two Values
subtitle: Behavior vs. Architecture, proof by extremes, Scope vs. Shape, Eisenhower's Matrix, and fighting for architecture.
description: 30 deep-drilling interactive questions exploring the two values of software, why structure outranks current function, the scope-vs-shape cost driver, Eisenhower's Urgency/Importance matrix, and the developer's duty as a stakeholder.

questions.prompt: What are the two distinct values that every software system provides to its stakeholders, and which one does Robert C. Martin prove is the greater value?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: Behavior (urgent functionality) and Architecture/Structure (ease of change); Architecture is the greater value because without it the system eventually becomes impossible to adapt and therefore useless.
options.explanation: Correct! Behavior makes or saves money today, but Architecture keeps the software 'soft' so it can continue to be useful as requirements inevitably change.

options.text: Behavior and Architecture; Behavior is the greater value because a beautifully structured system that doesn't satisfy current requirements generates zero revenue.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Martin specifically uses the logical tool of examining the extremes to prove that a broken system that is easy to change remains continually useful, whereas a working system that cannot be changed becomes useless as soon as requirements shift.

options.text: Performance and Security; Security is the greater value because data breaches destroy stakeholder trust.
options.explanation: Incorrect. While important quality attributes, Chapter 2 specifically contrasts Behavior (function) and Architecture (structure/flexibility).

options.text: Source Code and Documentation; Documentation is the greater value because developers rotate off projects.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chapter 2's 'Tale of Two Values' is strictly about Behavior vs. Architecture (Structure).

questions.overall_explanation: Every software system provides two values: Behavior and Structure (Architecture). Structure is the greater value because it preserves the ability to change.

questions.prompt: Complete Robert C. Martin's etymological breakdown of the word 'software' from Chapter 2:
questions.instruction: Type the missing words in the blanks.
questions.template: The word 'software' is a compound word composed of '{{1}}' and 'ware' (meaning product). Software was invented to be easy to change; if we had wanted the behavior of machines to be hard to change, we would have called it {{2}}.
questions.overall_explanation: Software exists specifically to make machine behavior 'soft' (easy to change). When architecture ossifies, software degenerates into hardware.

questions.prompt: According to Chapter 2, in a well-architected system, what should the difficulty of making a stakeholder-requested change be proportional to?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: Proportional only to the SCOPE of the change, and NOT to the SHAPE of the change.
options.explanation: Correct! Stakeholders view changes as a stream of requests of similar scope; good architecture is shape-agnostic so cost scales with scope rather than clashing with system shape.

options.text: Proportional to the SHAPE of the change, and NOT to the SCOPE of the change.
options.explanation: Incorrect. You reversed the two terms: when difficulty depends on the 'shape' of the change (jamming square pegs into round holes), development costs skyrocket out of proportion to scope.

options.text: Proportional to the total age of the codebase and the number of previous releases.
options.explanation: Incorrect. When Year 2 is much more expensive than Year 1 and Year 3 is much more expensive than Year 2 for changes of similar scope, that is the symptom of a rigid, shape-constrained architecture.

options.text: Proportional to the seniority of the product manager requesting the feature.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Effort should depend strictly on the functional scope of the change.

questions.overall_explanation: The gap between 'scope' (stakeholder view) and 'shape' (developer jigsaw puzzle view) is what drives the exponential growth in software costs.

questions.prompt: Map each quadrant of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Importance vs. Urgency Matrix to its priority rank and software value in Chapter 2:
questions.instruction: Click an Eisenhower quadrant on the left, then click its corresponding rank and software meaning on the right.

pairs.right: Critical architecture AND business-critical behavior that must be delivered right now
Software Architecture (structural cleanliness and flexibility—important, but never particularly urgent)
Routine Software Behavior / minor feature requests that managers often mistakenly elevate to Priority #1

pairs.left: 4th Priority: Not Urgent and Not Important
pairs.right: Trivial distractions and gold-plating that neither serve core requirements nor improve architecture

questions.overall_explanation: Architecture occupies Priority #1 and #2 (Important), whereas Behavior occupies Priority #1 and #3 (Urgent). Elevating #3 above #2 destroys the system.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four couplets of Eisenhower's Matrix in the exact priority order (1 = Highest Priority to 4 = Lowest Priority) defined in Chapter 2:
questions.instruction: Drag rows or use ↑ / ↓ buttons to put the four quadrants in order from 1 to 4.
questions.overall_explanation: Important items always take the top two spots (1. Urgent & Important, 2. Not Urgent & Important), placing Architecture ahead of Urgent-but-Not-Important features (#3).

questions.prompt: Audit this argument from a Product Director using Chapter 2's 'examining the extremes' logical proof:
questions.instruction: Choose the verdict and explain the logical proof by extremes in your own words.
questions.claim: A program that works 100% according to today's specification but cannot be changed is far more valuable to the business than a program that currently fails its specification but is easy to change.
key_concepts: Extreme 1: Works perfectly today but impossible to change -> becomes useless as soon as requirements change
Extreme 2: Does not work today but is easy to change -> you can make it work and keep it working as requirements change, so it remains continually useful
questions.model_answer: This is a dangerous fallacy refuted by Martin's proof by extremes. If a program works perfectly today but is impossible to change, it will stop working the moment requirements change and you won't be able to fix it—making it permanently useless. Conversely, if a program does not work today but is easy to change, you can make it work and keep it working as requirements evolve—so it remains continually useful.
questions.overall_explanation: Examining the extremes proves that ease of change (architecture) dominates current functionality (behavior) over any non-trivial lifetime.

questions.prompt: Classify each developer activity or concern into 'First Value: Behavior' or 'Second Value: Architecture (Structure)':
questions.instruction: Click an activity card, then click the value bucket it primarily serves.

items.text: Translating a stakeholder functional specification into machine instructions that calculate quarterly payroll taxes.
Opening a debugger when a machine violates a functional requirement and fixing the immediate bug.
Keeping policy modules shape-agnostic so new feature requests don't feel like jamming square pegs into round holes.
Ensuring the cost of a change remains proportional only to its functional scope rather than its structural shape.
Pushing back against management's attempt to elevate urgent-but-unimportant features above system modularity.

questions.overall_explanation: Many programmers mistakenly believe their entire job is implementing requirements and fixing bugs (Behavior), ignoring their higher duty to keep the system easy to change (Architecture).

questions.prompt: When someone objects to the 'proof by extremes' by saying 'No program is literally impossible to change,' how does Robert C. Martin respond?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: There are many systems that are PRACTICALLY impossible to change because the estimated cost of the change exceeds the business benefit of the change.
options.explanation: Correct! Once the cost of modifying a feature exceeds the profit or benefit that change would generate, the system is practically immutable in that area.

options.text: He argues that assembly-language and COBOL programs become physically read-only after 10 years.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The impossibility is economic (cost > benefit), not physical read-only storage.

options.text: He concedes the point and admits that behavior and architecture are of strictly equal value.
options.explanation: Incorrect. He stands firm that architecture is the greater value because economic immutability renders features dead.

options.text: He notes that hardware firmware cannot be patched once burned into ROM.
options.explanation: Incorrect. He is talking about everyday enterprise software systems where certain features or configurations become cost-prohibitive to alter.

questions.overall_explanation: Economic impossibility is real: the moment `Cost(Change) > Benefit(Change)`, the software is effectively frozen.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 warns against architectures that 'prefer one shape over another,' turning simple scope changes into square-peg/round-hole nightmares. Click the ONE line in this JavaScript notification dispatcher that hardcodes a rigid shape assumption, forcing edits to core workflow code every time a new channel (like SMS or Push) is requested:
questions.instruction: Click the flawed line of code below, then click Check Answer.

lines.text: if (!user.emailAddress || !user.smtpPort) throw new Error('Must be an SMTP Email user');
lines.explanation: FLAW: Welds the high-level workflow to the specific 'shape' of an SMTP Email user (`emailAddress`, `smtpPort`), making SMS, Webhook, or Push notifications square pegs in a round hole!
Delegation to polymorphic transport is clean once the shape check above is removed.

questions.overall_explanation: When core workflow logic demands `user.smtpPort`, the architecture prefers the 'SMTP email shape' over all other notification shapes.

questions.prompt: Complete the contrast between how stakeholders perceive change requests versus how developers in a rigid architecture experience them:
questions.instruction: Click each blank and pick the matching phrase from the word bank.
questions.template: From the stakeholders' point of view, they are simply providing a stream of changes of roughly similar {{1}}. From the developers' point of view, the stakeholders are handing them a stream of {{2}} that they must fit into a puzzle of ever-increasing complexity because the {{3}} of the system does not match the request.
questions.overall_explanation: Stakeholders think in scope ('just add one more notification channel'); developers suffer from shape mismatch ('our entire pipeline assumes SMTP email').

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental dilemma regarding business managers and software architecture described in Chapter 2?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: Business managers are not equipped to evaluate the importance of architecture—that is what software developers were hired to do, so developers must assert architecture's importance over the urgency of features.
options.explanation: Correct! Managers naturally focus on today's urgent features because they cannot see or evaluate internal architectural decay; developers were hired specifically to safeguard that structure.

options.text: Business managers intentionally want the system to become unmaintainable after Year 2 so they can justify larger departmental budgets.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Managers are furious when change estimates become unaffordably high—they want flexibility, they just aren't equipped to judge architectural trade-offs.

options.text: Business managers should be required to pass a JavaScript architecture exam before prioritizing the product backlog.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Evaluating architecture is the software development team's professional responsibility, not the business manager's job.

options.text: Developers should obey business managers unquestioningly because developers are employees, not stakeholders.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Martin explicitly states: 'Remember, as a software developer, you are a stakeholder. You have a stake in the software that you need to safeguard.'

questions.overall_explanation: Business managers cannot evaluate architectural health—that is the exact expertise developers and architects were hired to provide and defend.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words the paradox of how business managers react BEFORE vs. AFTER an architecture decays to the point where changes are unaffordable.
questions.instruction: Write 3–5 sentences in your own words. Click Check Answer for AI evaluation.
questions.placeholder:
Before decay, if you ask managers whether current features or future flexibility matters more...
Later, when you give them an unaffordable estimate for a change...
key_concepts: When asked upfront, business managers say current functionality is more important than later flexibility
Later, when they ask for a change and the estimated cost is unaffordably high, they are furious that developers allowed the system to reach a state where the change is impractical
Developers cannot use 'management told us to prioritize features' as an excuse; developers are responsible for fighting for architecture
questions.model_answer: When you ask business managers upfront whether they want flexibility, they say yes, but quickly qualify that current functionality is more important than future flexibility. However, if those same managers later ask for a change and your estimated cost is unaffordably high, they will be furious that you allowed the system to reach a point where the change became impractical. Because managers aren't equipped to evaluate architecture, developers must fight for architecture upfront rather than caving to short-term urgency.
questions.overall_explanation: Managers will pressure you to skip architecture today and then blame you tomorrow when changes become unaffordable—which is why you must stand firm today.

questions.prompt: Implement `prioritizeBacklog(items)` in JavaScript using Chapter 2's Eisenhower Matrix rules and Economic Impossibility threshold.
questions.instruction:
Given an array of backlog items `{ id, urgent, important, estimatedCost, expectedBenefit }`, return a new array of items that are economically viable (`estimatedCost <= expectedBenefit`), sorted by Chapter 2's 4-level Eisenhower priority:
1. `urgent && important`
2. `!urgent && important` (Architecture!)
3. `urgent && !important`
4. `!urgent && !important`
If two items share the same priority rank, preserve their original relative order. Each returned object should have `{ id, rank, viable: true }`.

test_cases.label: Architecture (#2: Not Urgent, Important) ranks ahead of Urgent Minor Feature (#3) and filters out Cost > Benefit
test_cases.call: prioritizeBacklog([{ id: 'minor-btn', urgent: true, important: false, estimatedCost: 500, expectedBenefit: 2000 }, { id: 'decouple-db', urgent: false, important: true, estimatedCost: 3000, expectedBenefit: 25000 }, { id: 'frozen-legacy', urgent: true, important: true, estimatedCost: 50000, expectedBenefit: 10000 }, { id: 'prod-outage', urgent: true, important: true, estimatedCost: 1000, expectedBenefit: 80000 }])

test_cases.label: All 4 quadrants sorted properly
test_cases.call: prioritizeBacklog([{ id: 'q4', urgent: false, important: false, estimatedCost: 10, expectedBenefit: 20 }, { id: 'q3', urgent: true, important: false, estimatedCost: 10, expectedBenefit: 20 }, { id: 'q2', urgent: false, important: true, estimatedCost: 10, expectedBenefit: 20 }, { id: 'q1', urgent: true, important: true, estimatedCost: 10, expectedBenefit: 20 }])

questions.overall_explanation: Eisenhower's Matrix places Not-Urgent-but-Important work (Rank 2: Architecture) strictly above Urgent-but-Not-Important feature requests (Rank 3).

questions.prompt: Which statements accurately reflect how Behavior and Architecture map onto Eisenhower's Matrix in Chapter 2? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.instruction: Select all correct options, then click Check Answer.

options.text: The first value of software—behavior—is urgent, but not always particularly important.
options.explanation: Correct! Behavior occupies positions 1 (Urgent & Important) and 3 (Urgent & Not Important).

options.text: The second value of software—architecture—is important, but never particularly urgent.
options.explanation: Correct! Architecture occupies positions 1 and 2 (the top two positions on the priority list).

options.text: The common failure of managers and developers is elevating Position 3 (Urgent and Not Important) to Position 1.
options.explanation: Correct! Failing to separate urgent-but-unimportant features from truly urgent-and-important ones causes teams to neglect important architecture.

options.text: Architecture belongs in Position 4 (Not Urgent and Not Important) until the system reaches 100,000 daily active users.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Architecture is ALWAYS important and sits in the top two priority positions from day one.

questions.overall_explanation: Because architecture is important (#1/#2) and many urgent feature requests are not (#3), elevating #3 to #1 starves architecture.

questions.prompt: Read these four statements from a Senior Software Engineer explaining why their team's codebase became unmaintainable. Click the ONE statement that violates Chapter 2's principle of developer stakeholder duty:
questions.instruction: Click the flawed statement below, then click Check Answer.

lines.text: 1. Sales, marketing, operations, and management all naturally fight for what they believe is best for the company.
lines.explanation: True—Chapter 2 explicitly notes that every department struggles for its priorities.

lines.text: 2. As software developers, we are NOT stakeholders; our duty is simply to code whatever features Product Management marks as urgent without arguing.
lines.explanation: FLAW: Martin explicitly writes: 'Remember, as a software developer, you are a stakeholder. You have a stake in the software that you need to safeguard. That's part of your role, and part of your duty.'

lines.text: 3. If architecture comes last and change becomes practically impossible, it means our development team did not fight hard enough for what we knew was necessary.
lines.explanation: Direct truth from the closing paragraph of Chapter 2.

lines.text: 4. Software architects are, by virtue of their job description, focused on creating a structure that allows features to be easily developed, modified, and extended.
lines.explanation: Accurately summarizes the architect's role in Chapter 2.

questions.overall_explanation: Software developers ARE stakeholders who were hired specifically to safeguard the structural health of the software in equal struggle with other teams.

questions.prompt: Why is the first year of software development often much cheaper than the second year, and the second year much cheaper than the third, even when stakeholders request changes of similar scope each year?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: Because the architecture prefers one shape over another, making each new feature request harder to fit into the existing jigsaw puzzle than the last.
options.explanation: Correct! When difficulty scales with the 'shape' of the system rather than the 'scope' of the request, costs grow out of proportion to feature size year after year.

options.text: Because cloud hosting and third-party SaaS APIs increase their unit pricing by 100% every year.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The escalating cost is engineering time and effort caused by architectural rigidity.

options.text: Because stakeholders intentionally ask for 10x larger scope in Year 3 while pretending the requests are small.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Martin specifically notes that stakeholders are providing a stream of changes of roughly similar scope.

options.text: Because JavaScript garbage collection slows down linearly with the age of the Git repository.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Runtime garbage collection has nothing to do with multi-year development cost growth.

questions.overall_explanation: Escalating year-over-year cost for same-sized features is the direct result of a shape-biased architecture.

questions.prompt: Refactor a shape-coupled report generator into a shape-agnostic JavaScript use case so that adding new output formats (JSON, CSV, HTML) has cost proportional only to scope.
questions.instruction:
Implement `generateSalesReport(records, formatter)` where:
1. `records` is an array of `{ item, amount, refunded }`.
2. Filter out any record where `refunded === true`.
3. Compute `totalRevenue` (sum of `amount` of non-refunded records) and `validCount` (count of non-refunded records).
4. Pass a shape-agnostic summary DTO `{ validCount, totalRevenue, items: validRecords.map(r => r.item) }` into `formatter(dto)` and return its result.

test_cases.label: CSV Formatter Plug-in
test_cases.call: generateSalesReport([{ item: 'Book', amount: 40, refunded: false }, { item: 'Pen', amount: 10, refunded: true }, { item: 'Course', amount: 160, refunded: false }], dto => `${dto.validCount},${dto.totalRevenue},${dto.items.join('|')}`)

test_cases.label: JSON Summary Plug-in
test_cases.call: generateSalesReport([{ item: 'License', amount: 99, refunded: false }], dto => ({ summary: `${dto.validCount} sold ($${dto.totalRevenue})` }))

questions.overall_explanation: Because `generateSalesReport` depends on a shape-agnostic `formatter(dto)` boundary, adding PDF, HTML, or CSV output requires zero modifications to the business rule.

questions.prompt: Audit President Dwight D. Eisenhower's classical observation as applied to software engineering in Chapter 2:
questions.instruction: Select the verdict and explain how it applies to Behavior vs. Architecture.
questions.claim: I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.
key_concepts: Urgent things are rarely of great importance, and important things are seldom of great urgency
First value of software (Behavior) is urgent but not always particularly important
Second value of software (Architecture) is important but never particularly urgent
questions.model_answer: This is architecturally sound and forms the backbone of Chapter 2's prioritization framework. In software, Behavior (a stakeholder's immediate feature or bug fix) screams with urgency but is often not strategically important, whereas Architecture (keeping the system easy to change) is critically important for survival but never screams with immediate deadline urgency.
questions.overall_explanation: Because architecture is never urgent, teams that prioritize by urgency alone will always starve architecture until the system collapses.

questions.prompt: Complete Chapter 2's description of the software architect's core focus and responsibility:
questions.instruction: Click each blank slot and select the matching phrase from the word bank.
questions.template: Software architects are, by virtue of their job description, more focused on the {{1}} of the system than on its {{2}}. Architects create an architecture that allows those features and functions to be easily {{3}}, easily {{4}}, and easily extended.
questions.overall_explanation: An architect's deliverable is a structure that makes features easy to develop, easy to modify, and easy to extend.

questions.prompt: What does Robert C. Martin mean when he says architectures should be as 'shape agnostic' as practical?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: The structure of the system should not favor one specific feature shape or delivery detail over another, so new requirements fit without forcing square pegs into round holes.
options.explanation: Correct! The more an architecture prefers one specific shape, the harder future features will be to fit into that structure.

options.text: All JavaScript objects should be untyped `any` dictionaries with no schema validation.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Shape-agnostic architecture means decoupling high-level policy from rigid structural assumptions, not abandoning domain data integrity.

options.text: UI components should only use circular Material Design buttons rather than rectangular cards.
options.explanation: Incorrect. 'Shape' in Chapter 2 is a metaphor for structural coupling in software architecture, not visual CSS geometry.

options.text: Every database table should store all columns as a single raw text blob.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Dumping everything into text blobs destroys structure rather than creating clean architectural boundaries.

questions.overall_explanation: A shape-agnostic architecture decouples core policy from specific delivery/storage shapes so new requirements slot in smoothly.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 states that healthy companies involve an ongoing struggle among equal stakeholders. Match each stakeholder group to what they naturally fight for and how developers must engage:
questions.instruction: Click a stakeholder group on the left, then click their primary focus on the right.

pairs.right: Fight for urgent current features and immediate customer-visible behavior (Positions 1 & 3)
Are stakeholders too, hired with a duty to safeguard the long-term maintainability of the codebase
Doubly responsible for fighting for system structure over raw feature urgency (Positions 1 & 2)

pairs.left: A Development Team That Never Pushes Back
pairs.right: Allows architecture to come last until change becomes practically impossible—and then gets blamed by management anyway

questions.overall_explanation: Every department struggles for what it sees as best for the company; when developers abdicate that struggle, the whole business loses its software asset.

questions.prompt: Triage these four real-world engineering tasks into their proper Eisenhower Matrix position from Chapter 2:
questions.instruction: Click each task card, then click the Eisenhower quadrant bucket it belongs to.

items.text: Fixing a broken checkout payment gateway that is currently blocking all live customer purchases.
Extracting direct SQL queries out of domain use cases behind a repository interface so next quarter's features stay easy to change.
Rushing a custom one-off banner animation requested by a manager for tomorrow's internal slide deck by hardcoding flags into the core router.
Debating for three hours whether to indent JSON config files with 2 spaces or 4 spaces when a formatter is already installed.

questions.overall_explanation: Distinguishing Quadrant 2 (Important Architecture) from Quadrant 3 (Urgent-but-Unimportant requests) is the core survival skill of a software team.

questions.prompt: According to Chapter 2, what do many programmers mistakenly believe is the ENTIRETY of their job?
questions.instruction: Select the single best answer.

options.text: Helping stakeholders turn requirements into code that makes the machine behave properly, and pulling out the debugger to fix bugs when it violates those requirements.
options.explanation: Correct! Martin writes: 'Many programmers believe that is the entirety of their job... They are sadly mistaken.' That covers only the first value (Behavior) while ignoring the greater second value (Architecture).

options.text: Drawing architectural boundary diagrams without ever writing production code.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The common mistake among programmers is focusing exclusively on behavior/debugging to the exclusion of structure.

options.text: Fighting with product managers all day so that no features ever ship.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Both values must remain high; the error is focusing only on behavior while letting structure rot.

options.text: Writing automated compilers and operating system kernels from scratch.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Chapter 2 addresses everyday application and system developers working with stakeholder requirements.

questions.overall_explanation: Implementing requirements and fixing bugs is only half the job—and the lesser of the two values.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence of events that occurs when a development team repeatedly elevates Eisenhower Position 3 (Urgent, Not Important) over Position 2 (Not Urgent, Important):
questions.instruction: Drag rows or use ↑ / ↓ buttons to order the progression from initial concession (1) to final blame (4).
items: Business managers press for an urgent but low-importance feature, and developers cave in, skipping architectural boundaries to ship it fast.
The system's structure becomes increasingly locked into one rigid shape, turning subsequent requests of identical scope into complex jigsaw puzzles.
Year-over-year development costs escalate until a newly requested business change costs more to implement than the benefit it could ever generate.
Business managers become furious at the development team for allowing the software to reach a state where the change is practically impossible.
questions.overall_explanation: Caving to Position 3 today guarantees you will be blamed when the system hits economic immutability tomorrow.

questions.bloom: Cost Proportional to Shape vs. Scope in JavaScript
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for a small-scope change: 'Let users export their invoice in Markdown in addition to PlainText.' Click the ONE line in this JavaScript `InvoiceService` where a rigid shape dependency forces you to modify the core domain class every time a format is added:
questions.instruction: Click the flawed line of code, then click Check Answer.

lines.text: constructor(id, lineItems) { this.id = id; this.lineItems = lineItems; }
total() { return this.lineItems.reduce((s, i) => s + i.amount, 0); }
export(type) { if (type === 'text') return `Invoice #${this.id}: $${this.total()}`; throw new Error('Unsupported format'); }
lines.explanation: FLAW: Hardcoding presentation format branches inside the core `Invoice` entity couples domain shape to every new export format.

questions.overall_explanation: Hardcoding `if (type === 'text')` inside the core entity means every small-scope export request forces intrusive edits to domain code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the key terms from Chapter 2's rule on change difficulty:
questions.instruction: Type the missing words in the two blanks.
questions.template: When stakeholders change their minds about a feature, the difficulty in making such a change should be proportional only to the {{1}} of the change, and not to the {{2}} of the change.
questions.overall_explanation: Scope vs. Shape: good architecture keeps change cost proportional only to scope, never to shape.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions follow directly from Chapter 2's 'examining the extremes' argument? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.instruction: Select all correct options, then click Check Answer.

options.text: A program that works perfectly today but cannot be changed becomes useless as soon as requirements change.
options.explanation: Correct! Since requirements always change, an unchangeable working program has a very short shelf life.

options.text: A program that does not currently work but is easy to change can be made to work and kept working as requirements evolve.
options.explanation: Correct! Ease of change allows you to both fix current defects and adapt to future requirements.

options.text: A system becomes practically impossible to change whenever the cost of change exceeds the benefit of change.
options.explanation: Correct! Even if code isn't theoretically immutable, exceeding the benefit threshold makes it economically unchangeable.

options.text: Developers should intentionally ship broken code to production to prove that their architecture is easy to change.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The extreme is a logical thought experiment to compare the two values; developers are responsible for keeping BOTH values high.

questions.overall_explanation: The thought experiment proves which value is more fundamental, while reminding developers that their duty is to keep both values high.

questions.bloom: Economic Viability & Shape Penalty Simulator in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Write a JavaScript function `simulateMultiYearChanges(requests, shapePenaltyFactor)` that models Chapter 2's year-over-year cost growth when an architecture is not shape-agnostic.
questions.instruction:
Given `requests` (an array of `{ name, scopeCost, benefit }`) and `shapePenaltyFactor` (a number >= 1, where `1` is a clean shape-agnostic architecture and `>1` compounds the cost on each subsequent change `i` as `actualCost = Number((scopeCost * Math.pow(shapePenaltyFactor, i)).toFixed(2))`), return `{ completedCount, blockedByCost: [...names], totalSpent }`:
- If `actualCost <= benefit`, the change is completed and `actualCost` is added to `totalSpent`.
- If `actualCost > benefit`, the change is practically impossible (Chapter 2): do NOT add to `totalSpent`, and push `request.name` into `blockedByCost`.
- Round `totalSpent` to 2 decimal places.

test_cases.label: Rigid Architecture (shapePenaltyFactor = 2.0 blocks later same-scope features)
test_cases.call: simulateMultiYearChanges([{ name: 'Year1-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year2-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year3-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year4-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }], 2)

test_cases.label: Clean Shape-Agnostic Architecture (shapePenaltyFactor = 1.0 completes all 4 years at constant cost)
test_cases.call: simulateMultiYearChanges([{ name: 'Year1-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year2-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year3-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }, { name: 'Year4-Feature', scopeCost: 1000, benefit: 5000 }], 1)

questions.overall_explanation: In a shape-agnostic architecture (`shapePenaltyFactor = 1`), four equal-scope changes cost $4,000 and all ship; with a 2x shape penalty, costs double each year until Year 4 ($8,000 cost > $5,000 benefit) becomes economically impossible.

questions.prompt: A Product Manager tells you: 'We don't have time to decouple the billing module right now—this new promotional badge is urgent for Friday's demo!' Using Chapter 2's Eisenhower Matrix and 'Fight for the Architecture', draft a concise, professional 3–4 sentence response.
questions.instruction: Write your response in your own words. Click Check Answer for AI evaluation.
questions.placeholder: Distinguish urgency (Position 3) from importance (Position 2) and explain how protecting the billing boundary keeps future changes affordable...
key_concepts: Distinguish urgency (Position 3: urgent but less important) from importance (Position 2: architecture is important though never urgent)
Explain that skipping the billing boundary today increases the 'shape' cost of every upcoming feature
Assert your role as an engineering stakeholder safeguarding the system's ability to remain soft and easy to change
questions.model_answer: I understand the promotional badge feels urgent for Friday's demo, but in Eisenhower's terms we need to be careful not to elevate an urgent-but-minor UI change (Position 3) above the important structural health of our billing module (Position 2). If we hardcode around the billing boundary today, we lock the system into a rigid shape that will make next month's pricing features exponentially slower and more expensive. As an engineering stakeholder, my job is to keep our software easy to change—so let's keep the clean boundary in place and scope Friday's demo badge so it fits cleanly.
questions.overall_explanation: Effective developers unabashedly advocate as equal stakeholders, framing architecture in terms of future change cost and business agility.

questions.model_answer: When a development team fails to fight for Chapter 2's Second Value (Architecture) and repeatedly elevates urgent-but-unimportant features (Eisenhower Position 3) over structural cleanliness (Position 2), the software loses its 'softness' and locks into a rigid shape. Once change difficulty depends on system shape rather than request scope, every new feature becomes a harder jigsaw puzzle—causing the developer productivity collapse toward zero seen in Chapter 1's Figure 1.4. Executives respond by multiplying headcount (Figure 1.1) and monthly payroll up to $20M (Figure 1.5), yet total output plateaus (Figure 1.2) and cost per line of code explodes 40x (Figure 1.3) until changes cost more than their business benefit.
questions.overall_explanation: Chapter 2 explains the behavioral and organizational root cause of the economic catastrophe measured in Chapter 1.
